content: Congenital infections, particularly cytomegalovirus (CMV), are among the most common causes of hearing impairment. These infections can lead to a range of neurological consequences, from isolated sensorineural hearing loss to severe destructive brain lesions. Postnatal onset of hearing impairment and a progressive course are also frequently observed. Children with congenital microcephaly of unspecified etiologies demonstrate an increased incidence of sensorineural hearing loss. Microcephaly is often associated with abnormalities in vision and the eyes. Exposure to the Zika virus in utero has been linked to significant neurological consequences. Reports from regions with active Zika virus transmission indicate that children with congenital Zika virus syndrome often, but not always, present with congenital microcephaly. Autopsy studies have confirmed the presence of the Zika virus in affected fetuses and infants, supporting the conclusion that the virus can have a profound detrimental effect on the developing brain. Early reports suggest that children with congenital Zika virus syndrome may also experience sensorineural hearing loss. However, due to limited follow-up data, the prevalence and clinical course of this condition remain unclear. Identifying the underlying cause of microcephaly is critical for determining the child’s prognosis, managing potential complications, and providing counseling for future pregnancies. In neonates with congenital microcephaly or disproportionately small head size relative to the face, a comprehensive history, physical examination, and neurological assessment—including hearing and vision evaluations—should be conducted to detect additional abnormalities potentially associated with Zika virus infection. These evaluations can help differentiate congenital infections from environmental or genetic causes of microcephaly. Hearing screening should be performed as early as possible, ideally before hospital discharge, especially in neonates born in areas with active Zika virus transmission. Screening should follow WHO guidelines for newborn and infant hearing screening and can be conducted using automated auditory brainstem responses (ABR) or otoacoustic emissions (OAE). In settings where physiological tests are unavailable, behavioral measures may be used. Vision assessment in newborns can be challenging, and an ophthalmologist should perform an ocular examination when possible. Neuroimaging abnormalities are common in children with congenital microcephaly, particularly when neurological signs or symptoms are present. These findings can help determine the underlying cause of microcephaly. In non-Zika virus settings, neuroimaging abnormalities have been observed in 80% of children with a head circumference below -3 standard deviations (SD) using computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). MRI alone has identified abnormalities in 88% of such cases. Common findings include cerebral calcifications, brain atrophy, ventriculomegaly, cerebellar and brainstem anomalies, cortical gyral abnormalities, and callosal abnormalities. Gyral abnormalities, such as polymicrogyria, pachygyria, or lissencephaly, are often diffuse but may be frontal-predominant. These patterns suggest that the Zika virus interferes with brain development rather than causing destruction later in development. Cerebral calcifications are frequently detected in congenital Zika virus syndrome, often subcortical in location. Other findings include brain atrophy, ventriculomegaly, cerebellar and brainstem anomalies, and cortical gyral abnormalities. These abnormalities can also be seen in other congenital infections, such as CMV, though the distribution and severity may differ. For example, intracranial calcifications in congenital CMV are typically subependymal rather than subcortical. Emerging evidence suggests that neuroimaging findings in congenital Zika virus syndrome may be more striking than those in other congenital infections. CT is more effective at identifying cerebral calcifications, while MRI provides higher resolution and better delineation of abnormalities in the cerebral cortex and posterior fossa. Either modality is sufficient to identify typical radiological features of congenital Zika virus syndrome. However, the utility of postnatal cranial ultrasound in this context is limited, as the peripheral distribution of brain calcifications in Zika virus syndrome may be difficult to detect. Additionally, the quality of cranial ultrasound depends on the size of the anterior fontanelle, which is often very small or closed in neonates with congenital Zika virus syndrome. Neonates with head circumference below -2 SD and disproportionately small head size relative to the face should undergo neuroimaging if Zika virus infection is suspected during pregnancy or if neurological signs or symptoms are present. For neonates with head circumference below -3 SD, neuroimaging should be performed unless there is strong evidence of a genetic or environmental cause of microcephaly. When neuroimaging is indicated, either CT or MRI can be used. If these modalities are unavailable, cranial ultrasound may be performed if the anterior fontanelle is adequately sized. Currently, there are no pathognomonic neurological findings for congenital Zika virus syndrome. Reported findings include cerebral calcifications, brain atrophy, ventriculomegaly, cerebellar and brainstem anomalies, cortical gyral abnormalities, and callosal abnormalities. Cerebral calcifications are commonly seen in congenital infections and some genetic disorders, such as Aicardi-Goutières syndrome. Neuroimaging findings should be interpreted in the context of other clinical and laboratory information. To attribute microcephaly or other neurological findings to in utero Zika virus exposure, other causes of congenital abnormalities must be excluded. However, there is no validated laboratory diagnostic test or commercial assay to confirm congenital Zika virus infection in neonates. Zika virus RNA has been detected by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) in the serum of neonates with perinatal transmission from the mother. Zika virus IgM has also been detected in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of infants with congenital Zika virus syndrome. Both RT-PCR and serology are recommended to determine congenital infection, as the sensitivity and specificity of these tests are still being established. Serological testing for TORCH infections should be performed in neonates with congenital microcephaly or disproportionately small head size relative to the face, particularly if Zika virus infection is suspected during pregnancy or if neurological signs or symptoms are present. Positive CMV serology in a neonate is not a reliable indicator of in utero CMV infection; diagnosis requires detection of CMV in urine, saliva, blood, or other tissues within 2-3 weeks of birth. Infants with congenital Zika virus syndrome are at high risk for complications, including developmental delay, seizures, hearing and visual impairment, excessive irritability, early-onset spasticity, swallowing difficulties, arthrogryposis, and hip dysplasia. Due to limited follow-up data, the long-term course of congenital Zika virus syndrome is not fully understood. However, children with congenital infections and/or microcephaly are at high risk for developmental delays and sensory impairments, particularly in the presence of abnormal neurological examinations or neuroimaging findings. Existing WHO guidelines for managing the sequelae of congenital Zika virus syndrome should be utilized for comprehensive treatment, including guidelines for epilepsy, spasticity, hearing, and vision. Families of affected infants should receive psychosocial support to address anxiety and distress. A multidisciplinary approach is essential for early interventions, neurodevelopmental support, and management of complications. Comprehensive neurodevelopmental assessments and supportive therapies should be provided for difficulties such as irritability, seizures, swallowing difficulties, spasticity, and hip dysplasia. Limited follow-up data are available for children affected by congenital Zika virus syndrome, with most cases reported in Brazil involving infants less than 12 months old. Retrospective data from French Polynesia have shown an increased incidence of microcephaly associated with a Zika virus outbreak, but follow-up data from that period are scarce. Follow-up management can be informed by existing guidelines for other congenital infections and microcephaly-associated neurodevelopmental conditions. Monitoring head circumference and conducting repeat neurological examinations can provide insights into brain growth and the likelihood of neurodevelopmental abnormalities. Findings may also aid in counseling families.
